header.title: De materia medica: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Dioscurides Pedianus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg0656.tlg001.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0656.tlg001.1st1K-gr: 'Boiled' renders ἀπολζεσθέντα, which is not a Greek word; probably a misprint for ἀφεψηθέντα.
'Idaean fingers': the text reads δαίους, taken as a slip for Ἰδαίους.
The Memphite stone has not been securely identified.
This 'wild rue' is generally taken to be harmal or Syrian rue (*Peganum harmala*), as the name *harmala* suggests.
*sēsamoeides*: a purgative plant whose identity is uncertain. 'Provokes sneezing' renders πταρμικούς τε ἐρεθίζει, probably for πταρμούς.
'Drawing forward [the foreskin]' renders *epagōgia*, procedures to lengthen a deficient foreskin.

nodes.text: 46 Some also call 'wild rue' the plant that in Cappadocia and in Galatia in Asia is called *mōly*. It is a shrub that sends up many rods from a single root, with leaves much longer and softer than those of the other rue, heavy-smelling; a white flower; and at the top little heads a little larger than those of garden rue, mostly made up of three parts, in which there is a yellowish, triangular seed, quite bitter to the taste; it is this that is used.

2 The seed ripens in autumn; it is suitable for dim sight, ground with honey, wine, hen's bile, saffron and fennel juice. Some call it *harmala*, the Syrians *bēssasa*, the Cappadocians *mōly*, since it keeps to some extent a resemblance to moly, being black in the root and white in the flower. It grows on hillocks and in places with good soil.

2 The leaves have the power, boiled in vinegar and drunk for forty days, to reduce the spleen; one should also plaster the spleen with the leaves ground fine with wine. It also helps strangury, hiccup and jaundice, and breaks up stones in the bladder. It is thought to be a contraceptive by itself, and when hung on [as an amulet] with a mule's hoof; and they say that for a contraceptive one should dig it up when the night or the day is moonless.

140 *Glykysidē* [peony]: some call it *pentorobos*, some 'Idaean fingers', and the root they call *paiōnia*, others *aglaophōtis*. Its stem grows two spans high, with many side-shoots; the male has leaves like those of the walnut, while the female has its leaves divided like alexanders. At the top of the stem it sends up pods like almonds; when these are opened, many small red seeds are found, resembling those of the pomegranate, and in the middle black, purplish ones, five or six.

2 The root of the male is about a finger thick and a span long, astringent to the taste, white; in the female the roots have seven or eight offshoots like acorns, as asphodel does. The root is given to women who are not cleansed after childbirth, and drunk in the amount of an almond it brings on the menses; drunk in wine it helps pains of the belly, and those with jaundice or kidney disease and those with pain in the bladder; boiled down in wine and drunk, it stops the bowels.

3 The apples too are juiced in the same way, but the juice from them turns out weaker; and the bark of the root is stripped off, threaded on a string and hung up for storage. Some boil the roots down in wine to a third, strain it and store it, using one *kyathos* [ladleful] for the sleepless and those in severe pain, and for those in whom they wish to produce insensibility when they are being cut or cauterised.

It purges by vomiting, bringing up matter of various kinds. It is also mixed into eye-salves that can clear away whatever darkens the pupils; applied as a pessary, it brings on the menses and destroys embryos; it provokes sneezing; kneaded with honey and barley-meal it kills mice; and boiled together with meat, it dissolves it. It is given to people fasting, by itself, and with *sēsamoeides* [sesame-like plant] and juice of *thapsia* [deadly carrot], and with *halix* [spelt groats] and honey-water, or porridge, or lentils, or broth; it is also made up with bread and baked.

or to alter the pores. 4 Hence the juice smeared on, or the fresh root rubbed on, makes patches of alopecia grow thicker with hair; and the root ground fine, or the juice, with equal amounts of frankincense and wax, removes black eyes and livid bruises; but one must not leave it on more than two hours, and afterwards foment with hot seawater. It also removes freckles; smeared on with honey it also clears *lepra* [scaly skin disease]; and the juice, smeared on with sulphur, bursts growths. It is also usefully smeared on those who have chronic conditions of the side or lung or feet or joints. It is also useful for drawing forward [the foreskin] in those who lack foreskin not as a result of circumcision, by raising a swelling which, when bathed and softened with emollients, fills out what is lacking of the foreskin.

4 Planted together with vines, at the root, it makes the wine from them purgative. People also sprinkle houses with it, believing it to be purifying; and so, when digging it up, they stand facing east, praying to Apollo and Asclepius and watching out for an eagle; for they say it flies over [them] not without danger: the bird brings death if it sees the hellebore being dug. One must dig quickly, because heaviness of the head arises from its exhalation; so, as a precaution, the diggers eat garlic beforehand and drink wine, and so come to less harm. Its core is removed, as with white hellebore.

140 The Memphite stone is found in Egypt near Memphis; it is the size of pebbles, greasy and variegated. It is reported that, ground fine and smeared on places about to be cut [or] cauterised, it brings on insensibility without danger.
